planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky, alkaline soil so winter freeze-thaw cycles complete the stratification; this legume resents rich, amended beds and performs best left alone on exposed limestone.

directions: Sow where the soil is thinnest and most alkaline, on exposed limestone bedrock or rubble with almost no organic buildup, in full sun — this is a true Nashville Basin cedar-glade specialist that disappears from garden beds with normal fertility or irrigation. Fragrant gray-green foliage spreads into a low, sprawling mound topped from midsummer into early fall by dense, cylindrical spikes of tiny magenta-purple flowers with bright gold anthers that open in a rolling band up the spike. Like other prairie clovers it fixes its own nitrogen and develops a deep taproot, so site it permanently as a seedling rather than attempting to move an established plant. Pair it with other glade specialists such as Echinacea tennesseensis or little bluestem in a rock garden or constructed glade bed that mimics its native thin-soil habitat.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat before a dormant fall sowing on thin, open, limestone-derived soil; this federally endangered legume cannot compete with taller vegetation or thatch, so the sowing site must be kept sparse and weed-free.

directions: Leafy prairie clover was federally listed as endangered in 1991 and survives naturally in only a handful of limestone cedar-glade and dry prairie remnants across Illinois, Tennessee, and Alabama, so growing it from nursery-sourced seed directly supports its ongoing recovery. It forms slender, upright, densely leafy stems topped from midsummer into early fall by compact cylindrical flower heads of pink-purple blooms that attract a range of small native bees. Give it unamended, thin, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun and keep competing vegetation mowed or cleared back, since it is quickly shaded out by taller prairie grasses and forbs in richer ground. Once established the deep taproot makes it quite drought tolerant, but it should never be divided or transplanted after its first season.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring into thin, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; established clumps can later be divided in early spring before new growth hardens off, since the milky latex sap makes seed propagation slow and inconsistent in cultivation.

directions: This naturally compact, glade-adapted variant of eastern bluestar is restricted to a few dozen cedar-glade and limestone-barren occurrences in the Nashville Basin of Tennessee and the Kentucky Bluegrass region, where it stays noticeably shorter and more tidy than the woodland-edge form of the species. In April it carries clusters of pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers above narrow willow-like foliage, and the whole plant turns clear gold in fall. It thrives on thin, rocky, alkaline soil that would be considered too poor and dry for the straight species, and good drainage is more important to its long-term survival in the garden than rich soil or supplemental watering. Use it in a sunny rock garden or gravel bed as a smaller-scale substitute for standard Amsonia tabernaemontana.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small plugs in spring into consistently damp, mineral-rich soil over limestone, such as the margin of a seep or the shaded edge of a glade seep-slope; standard dry garden beds are too dry for this species.

directions: Glade savory is a true habitat specialist, known from only a scattering of wet cedar glades and limestone creek seeps in the Nashville Basin, the Kentucky Bluegrass region, and two counties in Alabama, where it grows in open, mineral-saturated, calcium-rich ground that stays damp even through summer. Unlike most of its drought-tolerant glade neighbors, it needs a consistently moist, seep-like microsite with light shade for part of the day, making it a good fit for the wet margin of a rain garden or constructed glade seep rather than a typical dry rock garden. From late spring through summer it carries small, pale pink, two-lipped flowers typical of the mint family above low, mounding, aromatic foliage. Because its native habitat is so narrow and easily disturbed, source plants only from nurseries propagating from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected material.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Pour briefly boiling water over the hard, nutlet-like seeds before a fall direct sowing, or combine the hot-water treatment with winter cold-moist stratification; the thick seed coat otherwise delays germination for a year or more.

directions: Marbleseed is centered on the limestone prairies and cedar glades of the Nashville Basin, with scattered populations reaching into the Kentucky Bluegrass region, northwest Alabama, and the Ozarks, and it has become very rare outside Tennessee as glade habitat has been lost. Bristly, gray-green, hairy foliage covers an upright clump, and nodding clusters of small, creamy white to pale yellow-green tubular flowers open from late spring into summer, followed by the hard, pearly white, marble-like nutlets that give the plant its common name. It develops a long taproot and thrives in exactly the lean, rocky, excessively drained soil that defeats most garden perennials, so avoid fertile beds, mulch, or supplemental irrigation once it is established. Grow it among little bluestem or prairie dropseed in a dry, sunny limestone-glade planting where its unusual flower and seed structure can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Eastern Prairie Blue Wild Indigo (Glade Wild Indigo)

planting.note: Scarify the hard legume seed coat and sow in fall directly into its permanent, thin, rocky, alkaline position; like other baptisias it forms a woody taproot almost immediately and does not transplant well once past its first year.

directions: Formerly treated as Baptisia australis var. aberrans, this taxon is now usually recognized as its own species restricted to limestone and other calcareous glades and barrens of Kentucky, Tennessee, Georgia, Alabama, and North Carolina. It carries the same lavender-blue, lupine-like flower spikes as the familiar blue wild indigo, but on a noticeably shorter, more compact plant with leaflets held in a more vertical plane, and its tight, densely flowered raceme packs a disproportionately showy bloom onto a smaller footprint in April and May. Because it is adapted to thin, dry, rocky limestone soil rather than the deeper prairie loam preferred by the common species, it is a better match for a sunny rock garden, limestone outcrop planting, or small-space native bed. Expect two to three seasons for the deep taproot to establish before the plant reaches full flowering size, after which it is extremely long-lived and drought tolerant.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Sow directly onto thin, gritty, rocky limestone soil or a lean gravel-amended bed in spring; this diminutive succulent rots quickly in any soil that holds moisture and needs the sharp drainage of its native glade-rock habitat.

directions: Limestone fameflower is a very rare succulent endemic to limestone cedar glades of the Interior Low Plateau in Tennessee, Kentucky, and Alabama, with a disjunct presence in the Ozark Highlands, and it survives by rooting directly into shallow soil pockets on exposed limestone pavement where almost nothing else can grow. A low basal rosette of narrow, cylindrical, succulent leaves sends up wiry stems bearing small, star-shaped, magenta to purple flowers that open only in the heat of the afternoon and close again by evening. It is being evaluated for green-roof and rock-garden use because of its extreme tolerance for shallow, droughty, mineral soil, and in cultivation it should be treated much like a hardy sedum or sempervivum rather than a conventional perennial. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining grit or crushed limestone screenings, and avoid any organic mulch that would hold moisture against the crown.
